task.background: You are the navigator of a boat in a two-dimensional simulator. A dashed reference route connects mandatory checkpoints in order. Your job is to follow this route, enter every checkpoint circle without passing it by, and finally stop inside the last circle. The route is the intended path between checkpoints, not merely decoration. The current checkpoint is the next mandatory gate, not a reason to shortcut a bend. No obstacles, wind, or sideways drift exist in this simulation. The world pauses while you decide. The boat executes one selected target speed and heading for the specified simulation duration before you receive a fresh observation.
task.current_goal: Enter the current checkpoint circle; keep moving through it.

route.near_route_direction: 10.165 degrees right of the current sampled bow

execution.frame: Every position is relative to the boat NOW: ahead/behind and left/right. The route and checkpoints are fixed in the world.
execution.speed_rule: A changed target starts constant acceleration immediately and reaches its target in 0.5 s; zero time is instant. Keeping the same target continues its remaining ramp.
execution.heading_rule: A changed heading target turns smoothly from the current yaw and arrives with zero yaw in 0.5 s; zero time is instant. The heading offset is set ONCE relative to the sampled bow. Keeping the same WORLD target continues its remaining turn.
execution.current_heading_command: 10.742 degrees left of the current sampled bow

action.instructions: Route segments are ORDERED, even where they cross or run beside each other. ordered_route_ahead ends at the CURRENT mandatory checkpoint; follow that segment first. after_checkpoint_preview belongs to the NEXT segment: use it to anticipate braking and turning, not as a shortcut or a replacement for the current checkpoint. A checkpoint may require a near U-turn. After a checkpoint switches, the new route may be behind the bow; reduce speed and turn toward it rather than moving fast while the bow swings. When already outside the preferred tracking distance, that distance is temporarily unattainable: compare END distance reductions to recover toward the active line. Do not keep crawling parallel to an offset line merely to avoid a corrective turn. The near_route_direction points toward the first upcoming point on the active curve; distant checkpoints must not pull you across a bend. Use the longer SAME-command lookahead as a warning of imminent overshoot or leaving the route. Actual execution still lasts only the stated action duration and replans afterward. When a high-speed command would soon depart the curve, choose a slower approach before the turn. Aim to keep the whole movement within task.preferred_tracking_error_m of the reference line. This is a soft tracking preference, NOT the checkpoint arrival radius. Prefer a smaller-speed choice if needed to satisfy that tracking preference, while avoiding unnecessary crawling. When multiple choices have comparable tracking and end alignment, take the one with greater route advance. Also inspect END BOW ALIGNMENT and END YAW: an endpoint close to the line is not enough if the bow points across it or the boat is still rotating away. Prefer ending aligned with the local reference direction and with little residual rotation, while continuing useful progress. Slow before turns rather than alternate large left/right commands at high speed. Each candidate reports its geometric route error and along-route progress over the SAME action duration. Smaller route-error distances mean closer tracking; larger forward along-route advance means less completion time. Compare these jointly: do not crawl for a negligible error reduction, and do not accept large deviation merely for speed. Choose ONE combined target speed and target heading for the next action. First ensure the current checkpoint is not missed and the final stopping condition is respected. Follow the NEAR portion of the ordered reference route closely. Within those requirements, finish the route in as little SIMULATION TIME as possible: choose useful forward progress rather than unnecessary stops, crawling, or detours. Go fast on aligned straight sections; slow only as needed to negotiate a bend, correct deviation, enter a checkpoint, or stop. The candidate midpoint and endpoint describe curved motion in the CURRENT observation frame. A heading target is not an immediate movement direction. Account for existing rotation, the speed ramp, and the end yaw before choosing another turn. If the current checkpoint is behind, recover toward it rather than following the route beyond it. Checkpoint: enter its circle while moving; no parking. Final approach: enter and brake to remain inside. Final parking: target zero speed until actual speed satisfies the threshold. A stopped boat outside the final circle must approach, not repeatedly choose zero speed.
